Chapter 2: The Nature of Resilience and How It Grows
After the initial shock of loss, you might find yourself asking, "How do I move forward from here?"
The answer isn’t about big, dramatic changes or sudden bursts of strength. Instead, it lives in those small, everyday choices you make—one after another.
We often think of resilience as something you’re either born with or not. But here’s the good news: resilience can actually be grown and nurtured, day by day.
For one woman facing an entirely new reality, her journey with resilience started with giving herself permission. Permission to feel, to grieve, and importantly, to ask for help. She realized that trying to bottle up the pain only made it harder to heal.
So, she let herself acknowledge every emotion—no matter how tough. There were days when sadness felt overwhelming, and others when anger or guilt took center stage. Each feeling had its own space, and none of them needed to be hidden away.
During this time, a close friend became her anchor. Instead of offering quick fixes or empty words, this friend simply listened. Sometimes, they just sat together in silence. Other times, they swapped stories or chatted about the most ordinary things.
That steady presence was a reminder that support doesn’t always mean having the right words—sometimes, just being there is enough.
It became clear that resilience isn’t about dodging pain. It’s about learning how to live with it.
A lot of us imagine that people who cope well with loss must be extra strong or unshakeable. In reality, true resilience is built through vulnerability—by letting yourself feel, reaching out, and accepting help when you need it.
Here’s something to watch out for. Research shows that people often slip into a trap called “personalization,” blaming themselves for things they couldn’t control. This woman found herself replaying the day her husband died, wondering if she could have changed the outcome.
Over time, she learned to challenge those thoughts and recognize that some things are simply out of our hands.
Another trap is “pervasiveness”—the idea that one tragedy ruins everything. In the depths of grief, it’s so easy to see only darkness.
But as days passed, she started noticing little glimmers of light. Maybe it was a child’s laughter, a friend’s gentle kindness, or a quiet walk outside. These moments reminded her that, even in loss, not everything was lost.
The third trap is “permanence”—that fear that the pain will never go away. In those early days, it truly felt endless. But as time went on, she realized that grief can shift and change. Some days were still hard, but there were also moments of peace, and even joy.
So, building resilience isn’t about erasing the pain. It’s about finding a way to carry it forward. It’s a process of adapting, of learning to live with a new reality. For her, it meant building new routines, seeking support, and allowing herself to hope for brighter days ahead.
Over time, she discovered something powerful: resilience isn’t a fixed trait. It’s a skill—and with practice, anyone can get stronger at it.
